newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU Commission dismisses German budgetary claim.
newsitem.headline: EU Commission dismisses German budgetary claim.

text.p: The European Commission on Monday dismissed German criticism that it is paying too much into the European Union's central budget, saying the construction of Europe was not an accounting exercise.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel was quoted on Saturday as saying that Germany was paying a net 20 billion marks ($10.7 billion) each year to the 15-nation bloc and said Bonn would ask that the annual contribution be reduced by about seven billion marks.
"We don't speak about net contributions. This is not in line with the European construction approach as we view it," Commission spokesman Thierry Daman told the Commission's daily news briefing.

Net constribution is the difference between what a country pays into the EU budget as a percentage of mainly its VAT (Value Added Tax) revenue and what it gets in the form of farm subsidies, regional development funds and other grants.
Because of its size and wealth, Germany is by far the largest contributor to the EU budget, which will amount to almost 82 billion European currency units ($87 billion) this year.

But like former British Prime Minister Margareth Thatcher in the 80s who successfully fought to recover a large share of the money paid into EU coffers, Germany is increasingly arguing that the gap has become too big.

From the government coalition to the opposition Socialist Party there is a general belief that there must be a revision as the country struggles with unification costs and fears that an enlargement of the Union to eastern Europe will increase its burden.
Waigel is also desperately searching for ways to cut the country's budget deficit to qualify for the launch of the bloc's single currency, the euro, in 1999.
"Germany, after unification, can no longer be classified as such a prosperous country as it was before," Waigel told the weekly news magazine Der Spiegel.
"We pay 0.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). The limit should be lowered to 0.4 percent. That would be seven billion marks less," he said.

The issue of national contributions to the EU budget will be discussed in 1999 when the bloc decides its future financing especially in light of the expected enlargement to include Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Estonia, Slovenia and Cyprus.

Waigel warned that Bonn would block the reform of the bloc's structural funds -- which benefits mainly the bloc's poorer members --- if the other EU nations resisted its demands for a fairer system of funding.

Before East and West Germany united in 1990, West Germany was one of the richest countries in the EU, although it has now slipped in the rankings. Bonn has pumped in more than one trillion marks to rebuild the delapidated formerly communist east. $1 = 1.856 marks $1 = .943 ecus
